title: GST/HST Rates by Province in 2026: Complete Canadian Sales Tax Guide
excerpt: Complete 2026 guide to GST, HST, PST, RST, and QST rates across every Canadian province and territory. Includes Nova Scotia's new 14% HST rate, registration thresholds, filing tips, and ITCs.
content:
Canada's sales tax landscape is a patchwork of federal and provincial levies that every business owner needs to understand. Whether you sell goods online from your home office in Alberta or operate a chain of restaurants across Ontario, the taxes you charge — and those you can claim back — depend entirely on where the transaction takes place.

This guide covers every GST/HST rate by province for 2026, explains how PST, RST, and QST fit in, and walks you through registration, filing, Input Tax Credits, and compliance. Note: Nova Scotia reduced its HST from 15% to 14% effective April 1, 2025 — the first provincial rate change in over a decade.

What Are GST and HST?

[[CTA_CONSULT]]

The Goods and Services Tax (GST) is a 5% federal value-added tax charged on most goods and services sold in Canada. It is administered by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA).

The Harmonized Sales Tax (HST) merges the federal GST with a provincial sales tax component into a single rate. Five provinces currently use HST:

| Province | HST Rate | Federal Portion | Provincial Portion | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Ontario | 13% | 5% | 8% | | New Brunswick | 15% | 5% | 10% | | Newfoundland and Labrador | 15% | 5% | 10% | | Nova Scotia | 14% | 5% | 9% | | Prince Edward Island | 15% | 5% | 10% |

In provinces that do not participate in the HST framework, businesses must charge the 5% GST separately. Some of those provinces also levy their own Provincial Sales Tax (PST), Retail Sales Tax (RST), or Quebec Sales Tax (QST).

2026 Sales Tax Rates: Every Province and Territory

The table below shows the complete sales tax picture for 2026. Use it as a quick reference when setting up your invoicing, e-commerce checkout, or point-of-sale system.

| Province / Territory | Tax Type | GST | PST / RST / QST | HST | Total Rate | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Alberta | GST only | 5% | — | — | 5% | | British Columbia | GST + PST | 5% | 7% PST | — | 12% | | Manitoba | GST + RST | 5% | 7% RST | — | 12% | | New Brunswick | HST | — | — | 15% | 15% | | Newfoundland and Labrador | HST | — | — | 15% | 15% | | Northwest Territories | GST only | 5% | — | — | 5% | | Nova Scotia | HST | — | — | 14% | 14% | | Nunavut | GST only | 5% | — | — | 5% | | Ontario | HST | — | — | 13% | 13% | | Prince Edward Island | HST | — | — | 15% | 15% | | Quebec | GST + QST | 5% | 9.975% QST | — | 14.975% | | Saskatchewan | GST + PST | 5% | 6% PST | — | 11% | | Yukon | GST only | 5% | — | — | 5% |

What Changed: Nova Scotia's HST Reduction

Effective April 1, 2025, Nova Scotia's HST dropped from 15% to 14%. The provincial component decreased from 10% to 9%, while the federal GST portion remains at 5%. This is the first HST rate change in Canada since Prince Edward Island joined the HST framework in 2013.

If your business sells to Nova Scotia customers, ensure your accounting software, invoicing templates, and e-commerce tax settings reflect the updated 14% rate. Transactions that straddle the April 1, 2025 effective date follow the CRA's standard transitional rules — the rate charged depends on when the consideration becomes due or is paid, whichever is earlier.

Understanding PST, RST, and QST

Not every province uses the HST system. Several provinces administer their own sales taxes alongside the federal GST:

Provincial Sales Tax (PST) — Charged in British Columbia (7%) and Saskatchewan (6%). These provincial taxes are administered independently of the CRA and require separate registration with each province.

Retail Sales Tax (RST) — Manitoba charges a 7% RST. Like PST in other provinces, RST is administered by the provincial government and has its own registration, filing, and remittance requirements.

Quebec Sales Tax (QST) — Quebec charges a 9.975% QST, administered by Revenu Québec. Businesses selling in Quebec must register for QST separately and file returns with Revenu Québec — not the CRA.

The key distinction: GST and HST are federal (or federal-provincial combined) taxes overseen by the CRA. PST, RST, and QST are purely provincial and may have different exemptions, thresholds, and filing deadlines than the federal system.

GST/HST Rates by Province

Alberta

Alberta charges only the 5% federal GST. There is no provincial sales tax, making Alberta the province with the lowest overall sales tax rate in Canada.

British Columbia

British Columbia applies a 5% GST and a 7% PST separately, for a combined rate of 12%. Certain items — such as food, children's clothing, and prescription drugs — are exempt from BC PST.

Manitoba

Manitoba levies a 5% GST and a 7% RST (Retail Sales Tax). The RST applies to most tangible personal property and certain services. Businesses must register with Manitoba Finance for RST collection.

New Brunswick

New Brunswick uses a 15% HST, combining the 5% federal GST with a 10% provincial component into a single harmonized rate.

Newfoundland and Labrador

Newfoundland and Labrador also applies a 15% HST, with the same 5% federal and 10% provincial split as New Brunswick.

Northwest Territories

The Northwest Territories charges only the 5% GST. There is no territorial sales tax.

Nova Scotia

As of April 1, 2025, Nova Scotia's HST rate is 14% (reduced from the previous 15%). The rate comprises 5% federal GST and a 9% provincial component.

Nunavut

Nunavut charges only the 5% GST with no additional territorial sales tax.

Ontario

Ontario applies a 13% HST, which breaks down as 5% federal GST plus an 8% provincial component. Ontario's HST rate has remained unchanged since it was introduced in 2010.

Prince Edward Island

Prince Edward Island charges a 15% HST, the combined rate of 5% federal GST and 10% provincial sales tax.

Quebec

Quebec uses a 5% GST alongside a 9.975% QST, for a combined rate of approximately 14.975%. The QST is administered by Revenu Québec, not the CRA, requiring a separate registration.

Saskatchewan

Saskatchewan charges a 5% GST and a 6% PST, totalling 11%. The provincial PST is administered by the Saskatchewan Ministry of Finance.

Yukon

Yukon charges only the 5% GST. Like the other territories, there is no additional territorial sales tax.

Calculating GST/HST for Goods and Services

When calculating GST/HST, start by identifying the province where the supply is made and the applicable rate. The formula is straightforward:

Tax Amount = Sale Price × Tax Rate

Example 1 — HST province: A $1,000 sale of goods in Ontario:
$1,000 × 13% = $130 HST. Total charged to customer: $1,130.

Example 2 — GST + PST province: A $1,000 sale in British Columbia:
$1,000 × 5% = $50 GST
$1,000 × 7% = $70 PST
Total charged to customer: $1,120.

Example 3 — Nova Scotia (updated 2026 rate): A $1,000 sale in Nova Scotia:
$1,000 × 14% = $140 HST. Total charged to customer: $1,140.

In provinces with separate GST and PST/QST, both taxes are typically calculated on the sale price independently — PST is not applied on top of the GST (except in Quebec, where QST is also calculated on the pre-tax price as of 2013).

GST/HST Registration Requirements

Every business that provides taxable goods or services in Canada must register for a GST/HST account with the CRA once its worldwide taxable revenues exceed $30,000 in any single calendar quarter or over four consecutive calendar quarters. This is known as the small supplier threshold.

Below this threshold, GST/HST registration is voluntary — but many small businesses choose to register anyway because it allows them to claim Input Tax Credits (ITCs) on their business expenses.

Key points about registration:

  • Mandatory registration is triggered the moment you cross the $30,000 threshold. You must register within 29 days.
  • Voluntary registration is available to any business, even if under the threshold.
  • Non-resident businesses selling to Canadian consumers may also need to register, particularly for digital products and services.
  • Registration can be completed online through the CRA's Business Registration Online (BRO) portal.

    • Input Tax Credits (ITCs)

    One of the biggest advantages of being GST/HST registered is the ability to recover the tax you pay on business expenses through Input Tax Credits (ITCs). ITCs directly reduce the net tax you owe to the CRA.

    Common expenses eligible for ITCs include:

  • Office rent and utilities
  • Professional services (legal, accounting)
  • Computer equipment and software
  • Marketing and advertising
  • Inventory and supply purchases
  • Vehicle expenses (business-use portion)

    • To claim ITCs, you must have valid documentation that includes the supplier's GST/HST registration number, the date, the amount of tax paid, and a description of the goods or services. Receipts must be retained for six years from the end of the tax year they relate to.

    Filing and Remitting GST/HST

    Once registered, businesses must file GST/HST returns on a schedule determined by the CRA — typically monthly, quarterly, or annually, based on your revenue.

    | Annual Taxable Revenue | Default Filing Frequency | | --- | --- | | Over $6 million | Monthly | | $1.5 million to $6 million | Quarterly | | $1.5 million or less | Annual |

    Returns can be filed electronically through the CRA's My Business Account, GST/HST NETFILE, or third-party tax software. Paper filing is also available but not recommended due to slower processing.

    The net tax you remit is calculated as: GST/HST collected − ITCs claimed = Net Tax. If your ITCs exceed the tax collected, you will receive a refund from the CRA.

    The Quick Method of Accounting

    The Quick Method is a simplified accounting option for eligible small businesses with annual taxable supplies of $400,000 or less (excluding zero-rated financial services). Instead of tracking ITCs on every purchase, you remit a flat percentage of your revenue (including GST/HST collected) based on your industry and province.

    Businesses that purchase relatively few taxable inputs — such as service-based companies — often save money with the Quick Method because the remittance rate is lower than the actual GST/HST rate. However, you cannot claim individual ITCs (except on capital equipment purchases over $30,000) when using this method.

    GST/HST Exemptions and Zero-Rated Goods

    Not all goods and services are taxable. The Excise Tax Act divides supplies into three categories:

    Taxable supplies — Most goods and services fall here. GST/HST applies at the standard rate.

    Zero-rated supplies — These are technically taxable but at a rate of 0%. Businesses can still claim ITCs on inputs used to make zero-rated supplies. Examples include basic groceries, prescription drugs, medical devices, and exports.

    Exempt supplies — No GST/HST is charged, and businesses cannot claim ITCs on inputs used to provide exempt supplies. Examples include most health and dental services, residential rent, most financial services, and childcare.

    Understanding the distinction matters: if your business makes primarily exempt supplies, you may not be eligible to register for GST/HST or claim ITCs at all.

    Impact of GST/HST on Business

    Sales taxes affect nearly every aspect of running a business in Canada — from pricing strategy and cash flow management to vendor relationships and customer experience.

    Pricing: Whether you display prices tax-inclusive or tax-exclusive influences customer perception. B2C businesses in HST provinces often include tax in shelf prices, while B2B businesses typically quote prices before tax.

    Cash flow: GST/HST collected from customers is held in trust for the CRA. Treating it as revenue is a common mistake that leads to cash crunches at filing time. Setting aside collected taxes in a separate bank account is a best practice.

    Compliance costs: Businesses selling across multiple provinces must navigate different rates, exemption rules, and potentially multiple provincial registrations. Using cloud accounting software like Xero or QuickBooks can automate rate selection and return preparation, saving time and reducing errors.

    Frequently Asked Questions

    How is the HST calculated in Ontario?

    Ontario's HST is 13%, calculated as a single tax on the sale price. It comprises a 5% federal GST portion and an 8% provincial portion. For a $500 purchase, the HST would be $500 × 0.13 = $65, for a total of $565.

    What is the current combined GST and PST rate in British Columbia?

    The combined rate in BC is 12% — a 5% federal GST plus a 7% Provincial Sales Tax (PST). These two taxes are calculated and remitted separately; GST goes to the CRA while PST goes to the BC Ministry of Finance.

    Which province has the highest combined sales tax rate?

    As of 2026, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Prince Edward Island share the highest rate at 15% HST. Nova Scotia, which previously matched them at 15%, now charges 14% HST following its April 2025 reduction. Quebec's combined GST + QST rate of approximately 14.975% is close to 15% but is administered as two separate taxes.

    What is the GST rate in provinces that don't use HST?

    The federal GST rate is 5% and applies uniformly across all non-HST provinces and territories: Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, Northwest Territories, Nunavut, Quebec, Saskatchewan, and Yukon. These jurisdictions may also levy their own provincial sales tax on top of the GST.

    How does Quebec's sales tax compare to other provinces?

    Quebec's combined rate is approximately 14.975% (5% GST + 9.975% QST). This places Quebec's total tax burden just below the 15% HST charged in New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, and PEI, but above Nova Scotia's new 14% HST rate. The QST is administered by Revenu Québec and requires a separate registration from the federal GST.

    When must I register for GST/HST?

    You must register once your worldwide taxable revenues exceed $30,000 over the last four consecutive calendar quarters or in a single calendar quarter. You have 29 days from the day you exceed the threshold to register. Voluntary registration is available below this threshold and allows you to claim Input Tax Credits.

    What is the Quick Method of accounting for GST/HST?

    The Quick Method lets eligible small businesses (annual taxable supplies of $400,000 or less) remit a flat percentage of revenue instead of tracking individual ITCs. It simplifies record-keeping and can result in tax savings for service-based businesses with low input costs.

    What changed with Nova Scotia's HST in 2025?

    Nova Scotia reduced its HST from 15% to 14% effective April 1, 2025. The provincial portion dropped from 10% to 9%, while the federal 5% GST portion remained unchanged. This was the first HST rate reduction in Canada since PEI joined the HST system in 2013.

    This article is current as of February 2026. Tax rates and thresholds can change — always verify with the CRA or a Chartered Professional Accountant before making business decisions. This content does not constitute professional tax advice.
